extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and publishers preparing or proofreading English prose
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules for punctuation and hyphenation in English text, intended to guide manuscript preparation, editing, and typesetting. Covers colons, semicolons, commas, apostrophes, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, and related conventions with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after salutatory phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter, and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "My dear Mr. Brown:"; "Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:" (See 43, 54).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between chapter and verse and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M."

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between place and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between the place of publication and the publisher's name in literary references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), II, 97."

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of colon with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He writes under the head of "Notes and Comments": "Many a man has had occasion..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon marks stronger division than comma
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative long-quotation examples show semicolons joining related but independent clauses; guidance notes that 'for' in certain cases should commonly be preceded by a semicolon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations use a semicolon between the different links if these consist of more than a few words closely connected, especially if individual clauses contain internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lists of countries with parenthetical clauses; multi-clause legal justifications: (1) despondent...; (2) out of work; etc.; names with titles separated by semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in Scripture references with chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references a semicolon is used to separate passages containing chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon is always placed inside the quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose of the comma
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous illustrative sentences demonstrating pauses, appositives, and internal breaks; citation of Century Dictionary definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma separating proper nouns of different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "To John, Smith was always kind;" "To America, Europe awards the prize..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before final conjunction in series (serial/Oxford comma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and,' 'or,' and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; or all the links in a longer series, or where individual links consist of several words; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Tom, Dick, and Harry;" "either copper, silver, or gold;" but omit when phrase is brief and close-knit: "a man good and noble and true."

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with clauses introduced by conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions like 'and,' 'but,' 'if,' 'while,' 'as,' 'whereas,' 'since,' 'because,' 'when,' 'after,' 'although,' especially if the subject changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example multi-clause sentence showing commas around subordinate clauses; but do not use a comma when the preceding clause is not logically complete without them or in brief close-welded phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma after introductory or parenthetical adverbs/particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions, adverbs, or phrases such as 'now,' 'then,' 'however,' 'indeed,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' etc., should be followed by a comma when beginning a sentence or clause to introduce an inference or explanation, and set off by commas when inserted into the middle of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Indeed, this was exactly the point..."; exceptions when connection is logically close or when such words directly follow a verb or qualify an adjective/adverb ('he was recovering very slowly indeed').

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with multiple preceding adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, it should not be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "the admirable political institutions of the country;" "a handsome, wealthy young man."

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to set off participial clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially those that contain an explanation of the main clause, should usually be set off by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Being asleep, he did not hear him;" "Exhausted by a hard day's work, he slept like a stone."

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'not' introducing antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' when it introduces an antithetical clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional clauses vs dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: For parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use commas and dashes together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comma: "The French, generally speaking, are..."; dash: see rules on dashes (151).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate identical or closely similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words even if sense or construction does not require separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Whatever is, is good;" "What he was, is not known;"

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma around qualifying/adjectival phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This harsh, though perfectly logical, conclusion;" "The most sensitive, if not the most elusive, part..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas to separate co-ordinate clauses modifying another clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more co-ordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "a shallow body of water connected with, but well protected from, the open sea;" "This road leads away from, rather than toward, your destination."

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate numbers and page references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers (e.g., two consecutive page numbers) and after digits indicating thousands; separate month and year with a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention;" "pp. 5, 6;" "1,276, 10,419;" "November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906." Note: some journals differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to indicate omission of words
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words whose repetition is not essential to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two;" but often constructions are smooth enough to omit commas and semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma in signatures and certain heading contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after an author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after an address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of signature formats with and without commas provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe marks omitted letters or figures
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of letters in contractions or of figures in a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "ne'er, don't, 'twas, 'takin' me 'at;" the class of '96.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming the possessive with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s (see 103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "a man's, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe; Jones's farm; Themistocles' era; for appearance' sake."

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare coinages with apostrophe-s
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals and of rare or artificial noun-coining is formed by adding an apostrophe and s; proper nouns of multiple syllables ending in a sibilant add an apostrophe alone; monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add -es; others add -s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "in the 1900's; in two's and three's, the Y. M. C. A.'s; Tommy Atkins' of England; but: the Rosses and the MacDougalls."

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash indicates sudden break or significant pause
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash denotes a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of dramatic uses: 'To be or not to be — that is the question;' 'Process — that is the magic word...' (John Wilson quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash for parenthetical clauses that are independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This may be said to be — but, never mind, we will pass over that;" "There came a time — let us say, for convenience, with Herodotus..." (see 136 on commas vs dashes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash to introduce explanatory or emphatic clause after repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas;"

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash when 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were the weapons...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken into clauses, the final summarizing clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Amos, with the idea that Jehovah is an upright judge ...; Hosea, whose Master hated injustice ...; Isaiah ... — these were the spokesmen ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash usage with side-heads and run-in heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether run in or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show typographic heading use: '2. The language of the New Testament. — The lexicons...' and notes about references taken from other sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash for 'to' connecting words or numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash for 'to' connecting two words or numbers, distinguishing en-dash and em-dash usage by context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'May–July, 1906' (en-dash); 'May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906' (em-dash); 'pp. 3-7' (en-dash); 'Luke 3:6 — 5:2' (em-dash). Guidance on omitting hundreds in ranges and journal exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before reference after a long direct quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title, or both) following a direct quotation consisting of at least one complete sentence in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I felt an emotion ...' — Thirty Years, I, 379. Poem followed by author and dash: '—Emerson, "To Ellen, at the South."'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse: dash should not pair with other points
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'Dear Sir:— I have...'; incorrect comma/dash mixes illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parentheses for enumerative markers and structured subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text; use specific schemes of notation for paragraphed subdivisions (A., I., 1., a), (i), etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '(1) advanced age, (2) failing health, (3) a desire to travel.' Formal indentation/notation scheme shown for syllabi and similar matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses reserved for less-integral or wholly irrelevant material
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses (see comma and dash rules), unless confusion would arise from using less distinctive marks or unless the contents are wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'He meant — I take this to be the (somewhat obscure) sense of his speech — that...' and citation parenthetical '(op. cit.)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets for editorial interpolations and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used to inclose an explanation or note, indicate an interpolation in a quotation, rectify a mistake, supply an omission, and for a parenthesis within a parenthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '[This was written before the publication of Spencer's book. — Editor.]' 'These [the free-silver Democrats] asserted...' and use in bibliographic citations and textual corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets for continued/continued-to-be-concluded notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like '[Continued]' and '[To be concluded]' at the beginning and end of articles or chapters should be placed between brackets (and set in italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '[Continued from p. 120]' '[To be concluded]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses indicate omission of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission of one or more words not essential to the idea being conveyed. For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence four periods, separated by a space (en-quad), should ordinarily be used, except in very narrow measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preceding line ends in a point, this should not be included in the four. For omitted paragraphs or complete lines in poetry insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads according to line length. Examples of prose and poetry omissions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis treated as part of the citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as part of the citation and consequently should be enclosed in the quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen at line breaks and in many compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word carried to the next line, and between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See section on divisions for line-break hyphenation; many examples of compounds follow in subsequent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'well-known author,' 'first-class investment,' 'high-school course,' 'four-year-old boy.' When components contain more than one word or are set in capitals, use en-dash (FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR). Do not hyphenate adverb '-ly' + participle combos: 'highly developed species.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use en-dash for multiword components or capitals in compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Where components are set in capitals or one of the components contains more than one word, use an en-dash instead of a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR; New York–Chicago freight traffic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by combining two nouns standing in an objective relation to each other (one component derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'mind-reader, story-teller, fool-killer, office-holder, well-wisher, property-owner.' Exceptions: brief common compounds like 'lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate present-participle + noun when forming new noun
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united with a noun to form a new noun with a meaning different from the two words separately, or with a preposition used absolutely to form a noun, should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, walking-stick, working-man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of book/house/mill/room/shop/work rules by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'book,' 'house,' 'mill,' 'room,' 'shop,' and 'work' are generally printed as one word when the prefixed noun has one syllable, hyphenated when two syllables, and two separate words when three or more, with a few exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'handbook, story-book, reference book; boathouse, engine-house, business house; commill, handmill, water-mill; bedroom, lecture-room, recitation room; tinshop, workshop.' Exceptions listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate maker/dealer and occupation compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker,' 'dealer,' and other occupation-denoting words should ordinarily be hyphenated; nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman.' Exceptions: brief common words like 'bookmaker, dressmaker.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rules for 'store' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Always hyphenate 'fellow-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate kinship compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'father,' 'mother,' 'brother,' 'sister,' 'daughter,' 'parent,' and 'foster' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'father-love (but: fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, foster-son.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'great-' compounds indicating degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great' indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'great-grandfather, great-grandson.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds of 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen (with some exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rules for 'skin' compounds by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with one-syllable words are printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'master-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated (exceptions noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'god' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'god' use a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'sun-god, rain-god.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'half', 'quarter' etc. + noun
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half', 'quarter', etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'half-truth, half-tone, half-year, quarter-mile.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes 'semi','demi','bi','tri' usually without hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Semi', 'demi', 'bi', 'tri' etc. do not ordinarily demand a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'semiannual, demigod, biweekly, bipartisan, tricolor'; exceptions: long or unusual formations like 'semi-centennial.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'self-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'self' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'self-evident, self-respect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations with 'fold' printed as single or separate words by syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are one word if the number contains one syllable; if more, print as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed with '-like' rules by syllable and proper noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixing 'like' to a noun are usually one word if the noun is one syllable (except when ending in /); if the noun has more syllables or is a proper noun, hyphenate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'childlike, homelike, warlike; eel-like, bell-like; American-like (but: Christlike).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate parts of titles (vice-, ex-, elect, general, lieutenant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of titles such as 'vice', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', and 'lieutenant' should be connected to the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'by-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds formed with 'by-' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'by-product, by-laws.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes co-/pre-/re-: hyphen when doubled vowel
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', and 're-' take a hyphen when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate; ordinarily they do not when followed by a different vowel or a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstal.' Exceptions: proper names, long/unusual formations, or to avoid ambiguity (Pre-Raphaelite, re-cover vs recover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles 'un-','in-','a-' usually without hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-','in-','a-' do not usually require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, asymmetrical.' Rare exceptions noted. The particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen except in common words ('nonessential' exceptions listed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'quasi-' prefixed words
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi' prefixed to a noun or adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate 'over-' and 'under-' generally
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (lengthy words, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'overbold, overemphasize, underfed, underestimate; but: over-soul, under-man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin prepositional prefixes usually no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin prepositions 'ante', 'anti', 'inter', 'intra', 'post', 'sub', and 'super' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'antedate, antechamber, antidote, international, intramural (but: intra-atomic), postgraduate.' Exceptions: 'ante-bellum, anti-Semitic, inter-university.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'extra','infra','supra','ultra' generally
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra', 'infra', 'supra', and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate fractional numerators/denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'two-thirds, four and five-sevenths, thirty-hundredths; but: one half (no hyphen) in certain constructions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate omitted common element
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have a common component omitted from all but the last word, indicate the omission by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces.' Note some writers view this as a Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen indicates prefix/suffix particle or syllabification
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or suffix as a particle or syllable not complete in itself; and to indicate syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-; the suffixes -chen and -kin.' Syllabification examples: 'di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common words to be hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific list of forty everyday compound words is provided which should be hyphenated and do not fall under previous classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (partial list): 'after-years, bas-relief, bee-line, bill-of-fare, birth-rate, blood-feud, common-sense, cross-examine, cross-reference, field-work, food-stuff, fountain-head, good-will, high-priest, ice-cream, ill-health, man-of-war, page-proof, pay-roll, post-office, son-in-law, subject-matter, terra-cotta, term-list, well-being, will-power.' (Full list in the source.)
